summary: FHSyncClient with NSTimer in background mode
description: FHSyncClient uses the NSTimer class to schedule server sync checks. iOS will kill this timer when app is backgrounded. Therefore, FHSyncClient cannot be used to reliably pull updates down from a server. As of iOS 7, the background mode "background fetch" is recommended for pulling such data. Apple recommends using NSURLSession when making network calls in a background fetch.
full_text:
FHSyncClient with NSTimer in background mode

FHSyncClient uses the NSTimer class to schedule server sync checks. iOS will kill this timer when app is backgrounded. Therefore, FHSyncClient cannot be used to reliably pull updates down from a server. As of iOS 7, the background mode "background fetch" is recommended for pulling such data. Apple recommends using NSURLSession when making network calls in a background fetch.

summary: Investigate how users currently use the Databrowser import/export feature in the Studio
description:
*What*
There is currently a lightweight import/export feature in the Studio for the Databrowser.
We need to understand:
- how users are/aren't using this feature
- if they aren't using it, why they aren't using it
- will the newer import/export feature usable from fhc be something they use?
- Is a UI on this newer import/export feature something they would use (or would they tend to use it from fhc)?
*Why*
- to ensure we aren't missing a valuable feature (UI on the import/export)
- to ensure we don't spend time on something that won't be of value
- to ensure there isn't any confusion about the difference between the 2 features
*Suggestions*
- engage with users (consulting) to get feedback
-- via slack & mail thread initially?
Timeboxing to 2 days.

summary: Begin monitoring Stack Overflow for AeroGear and FeedHenry questions
description:
I performed a few quick searches on Stackoverflow and found that there are some questions about AeroGear Unified push, FeedHenry mbaas, and the platform in general. They are very low traffic, but there is an audience in that forum already. We should be monitoring it and engaging in users there.
The goals of this ticket are : 
 * Define tags that we will search for and monitor
 * Set up mailing list email notifications for chosen tags 
 * Document on feedhenry.org what tags we are tracking and encourage people to use them
Additionally we could be able to reach out to consulting and sales as well. One idea I had was to encourage people who are evaluating the platform or using community grids to ask questions there. IE people who aren't paying for support have a community to support them.

summary: Investigate how to make API Mapper easier to stand-up
description:
*Story*
As a less technical user, I want to be able to easily create an instance of the API Mapper so that I can start using it immediately with no awkward setup steps.
*What*
Investigate how to make API Mapper easier to stand-up
*Why*
So less technical users can make use of the API Mapper
*Suggestions*
API Mapper currently requires a user to do the following to make use of it:
* Make the newly created service public 
* Visit the data browser, and upgrade the database so this application has it's own database. 
* Re-deploy the service
Understand the reasons for each of these steps, and identify ways of simplying them or removing them completely.
For example, if possible, we should deploy the Service with database by default and permissions set to Public.

summary: POC for horizontally scaling sync across clustered cloud apps
description:
Suggested approach:
* identify a set of tests (unit and/or manual) to use as regression tests while making changes
* identify all places in the Sync Server code that store dataset and/or sync data in-memory
* change in-memory locations to use redis (provided by the REDIS_ env vars) and using the redis cli (not fh.cache)
* re-run regression tests along the way to ensure sync behaves as expected.
* re-run same tests in a multi cpu environment and using node clustering to ensure the Sync Server code is horizontally scalable

summary: Setup & Document sync load test infrastructure in ec2
description:
*What*
Setup required instances in ec2 for performance load-runner based tests for the sync framework.
Any setup done should be documented to allow future load testing to be done without having to re-setup from scratch.
*Why*

summary: Document fix for duplicate sync issue
description:
h3. Overview
The resolution to RHMAP-12565 was that this was an expected feature of the platform. However, this issue might appear more so we should document it.
As the issue would be noticable on the cloud app side it could be documented in the README for 
It could also go into `guides/server-side-developer-guide/sync_service.js` in the documentation.
h3. Todo
The issue itself was that a client application had a syncFrequency of 120 seconds, due to this it was expected that the list function on the cloud would only be called every 120 seconds.
However, the cloud has its own syncFrequency which defaults to 10 seconds, this resulted in the list function being called twice every 120 seconds, increasing server load.
By updating the syncFrequency of a dataset on the cloud to match the syncFrequency of the dataset on the client this duplication is removed.

*How*
Change the create response handler to do a sync every 10 seconds until the updates are seen as applied and continue (or failed and stop the test)
Do the same for the update response handler

summary: Update the sync client to mark pending inFlight records as crashed after X number of sync loops
description:
*What*
Update the sync client to mark pending inFlight records as crashed after X number of sync loops
*Why*
This client change is to support a backend change where the server will respond early after accepting pending records, rather than accepting *and* processing pending records then responding.
In this scenario it is possible for the cloud app to crash after accepting the pending records and responding, but before the pending records are processed. Therefore, it is currently possible in the client for pending inFlight records to be stuck in that state indefinitely.
The only way currently to get those records to be resent is to mark them as crashed, which would happen if the error callback is called for a sync call
 For example, if the cloud app goes offline, all pending records on the client, including already inFlight records, will be marked as crashed.
*How*
Suggesting adding a new config for the number of sync loops to wait before marking an inFlight change as crashed.
This check should happen with every successful sync loop e.g. if the config value is 10, only mark pending inFlight records as crashed if they've been inFlight for 10 *successful* sync loops.

*Why*
This client change is to support a backend change where the server will respond early after accepting pending records, rather than accepting *and* processing pending records then responding.
In this scenario it is possible for the cloud app to crash after accepting the pending records and responding, but before the pending records are processed. Therefore, it is currently possible in the client for pending inFlight records to be stuck in that state indefinitely.
The only way currently to get those records to be resent is to mark them as crashed, which would happen if the error callback is called for a sync call
 For example, if the cloud app goes offline, all pending records on the client, including already inFlight records, will be marked as crashed.
*How*
Suggesting adding a new config for the number of sync loops to wait before marking an inFlight change as crashed.
This check should happen with every successful sync loop e.g. if the config value is 10, only mark pending inFlight records as crashed if they've been inFlight for 10 *successful* sync loops.

summary: When server crashes for less than one sync loop after immediate response the client should have a forever inFlight record
description:
Currently, in the case where the sync server responds immediately with no updates ( and does not stay down for at least one sync loop, the client will mark the dataset as inFlight and not have a reason to mark it as crashed until the server goes down, which could be never (or at least a very long time). This will mean the data is never persisted.
We should have a test for this functionality, using a mock sync server.

summary: Implement a queue factory to create mongodb-backed queues
description:
h3. Why
In order to scale the sync server, we need to allow sync requests to be processed by multiple processes. The best way to do it is to use queues. We also need persisted queues and HA to make sure the data won't be lost if the process crashes. Based on those requirements, we need to implement a queue backed up by mongodb. (We don't have HA for redis at the moment)
h3. What
Implement a queue factory can create queues based on a given name. Each of the queue should have the following interfaces (minimum):
* addJob - add a new job to the queue
* process - register a worker to get the oldest job off the queue and process it
The queue should be backed up by mongodb.
h3. Other considerations
For testing purpose, we should have a queue implementation that is in-memory.

summary: Allow the client sync frequency to be set by the server
description:
Currently an issue pops up regularly around users believing that setting the sync frequency on the client would also set the sync frequency of the dataset on the server. This is not the case and can cause two sync loops on the server each sync frequency if the client frequency is less than the server frequency.
If we were to allow the sync frequency for a dataset that is set on the server to be passed down to the client, we might be able to remove the misunderstanding by not needing users to set the sync frequency on both.
Setting the sync frequency for a dataset on the client would take precedence over the server sync frequency, allowing clients to decide to sync less often if they choose to.

description:
h3. Why
We need the handler to handle the syncRecords calls. It should use cached data when possible to reduce the number of calls to the backend database.
h3. What
The handler should:
* Try to get the dataset records out of redis
** If there is, use that to compare with the records, and after getting the delta, iterate through all those records, and if any of them is in the applied_but_not_in_cache collection, or if in the pending queue, remove them from the delta. This way the client will keep its value. See for sample gist
** The global hash should be from the last sync loop

Therefore this situation should only happen if something happens redis (flush?) between the sync loop and the syncRecords call from the client.

summary: Assert that getUID will retrieve the new UID of a record after a successful creation
description:
When a record is first created in the client, it is given a temporary UID which is the hash of the record. Once the record has been successfully created on the server this will be replaced with a MongoDB record uid.
The getUID function in the client API is supposed to map between these. For example, providing the hash of the created record should do one of two things:
* If the record has not been persisted on the server, return the hash of the record as that is still it's UID.
* If the record has been persisted on the server, return the MongoDB UID of the record as that is now the records actual UID.

summary: Assert the behaviour of scaling the current sync server
description:
Taken from sync doc:
{code}
If the current sync server code were horizontally scaled (e.g. via node.js cluster workers), the following would happen:
Depending on the number of active Clients and number of Cluster Workers, there may be unnecessary syncs happening for datasets. For example, if 3 Clients make a call to a different worker (load balanced) at 0, 1 and 2 seconds, those workers will mark the DataSet Client for sync at 10, 11 & 12 seconds respectively. This could cause unwanted load on the DataSet Backend as it does 3 syncs (doLists) in quick succession even though the sync frequency should only be 10 seconds.
After the above scenario, there may also be inconsistency on the Clients depending on which worker their next request gets through to. For example, if there was an new record added between the 10 & 11 second sync, those 2 workers will have a different dataset hash. Depending on which worker each Client gets load balanced to next, they may get the correct latest data, or may be told to delete the record that the worker think exists.
{code}
We should use this behaviour to create a test that would currently fail, where the sync server is clustered with two workers. The idea is that once the horizontal scaling work has been completed, this test should pass.

summary: Add a cleanup task for each of the sync queues in mongodb
description:
*What*
Add a cleanup task for each of the sync queues in mongodb
*Why*
The mongodb-queue module [1] keeps all queued jobs in mongodb, even after they have been 'taken' from the queue and processed.
Once processed and acked, they are marked as 'deleted'.
There is a 'cleanup' function that will remove any deleted jobs [2], but this must be manually invoked.
*Suggestions*
* -call cleanup after each ack of a job-
* -add a node-cron job that periodically calls cleanup for each queue-
* -if we want to keep all jobs as an audit log for a particular period of time, we could use node-cron to send a delete query to mongodb for jobs that are deleted & older than a certain time (e.g. 1 day). This approach would need to know about the inner workings of the mongodb-queue module and the collection(s) it uses-
* add config values for the time to keep complete jobs in the queue (as an audit log). On startup, run a query for each queue to remove any old jobs, and set an interval for it to be run again at a regular interval.
[1] 
[2]

summary: Change the sync logger to allow passing in a logger implementation
description:
*What*
Change the sync logger to allow passing in a logger implementation
*Why*
The current logger in the sync framework [1] is a wrapper around winston.
There are 2 problems with this approach:
* there is no way for a different logger used by a developer to be re-used by the sync framework, meaning potentially 2 different formats of logging in the app logs
* the logging wrapper only has a single logging function, doLog, rather than following a standard interface e.g. logger.error, logger.warn, logger.info. The way to do different log levels is to pass in a string as the 2nd parameter e.g. 'error'
*Suggestions*
* figure out what the most popular logger is in node.js (console.log?), and seeing how logging in modules is usually handled
* support the interface of this logger, meaning most developers can pass in an instance of that logger
* suggest in the docs to wrap any other loggers to conform to that interface before passing in (or let a default logger of our choice do logging)
[1]

summary: add the implementation for init, stop and stopAll
description:
h3. Why
In order to keep the API backward compatible, we need to implement the sync.init, sync.stop and sync.stopAll API
h3. What
Add implementations for the syn.init, sync.stop and sync.stopAll API
h3. Suggestsions
For sync.init, we can save a document to a new collection for the given dataset.
For sync.stop, we can remove the document from the collection for the given dataset.
For sync.stopAll, we can remove all the documents from the collection.
Then the sync & syncRecords API should be changed to check the collection to make sure the given dataset exists before continuing. If the document doesn't exist, they should return error. 
We should do the same for the sync scheduler to make sure if the dataset is stopped syncing, there should be not requests put on the queue.

summary: Investigate how to do realtime sync via websockets
description:
*What*
Investigate how to do realtime sync via websockets
*Why*
Both the current sync framework (fh-mbaas-api <=6), and the sync framework changes to support horizontal scalability are 'eventual sync' implementations.
This means any changes applied on the client will eventually be applied to the dataset backend. These changes will also eventually be propagated to any other active clients.
A recommendation from [~jfrizell@redhat.com] is to figure out the touchpoints for integrating websockets, with the intention of moving to realtime sync, as it may be a valueable feature of sync.
*Suggestions*
* Identify any sync APIs that may have to change
* Identify any config that is based on their being a sync loop (e.g. sync_frequency, crash retry count)
* Identify how much of the client & server code would be replaced by the websockets layer
* How to maintain backwards compatibility for Environments that don't support websockets
* How to notify multiple clients of updates as they are processed
Based on the report produced by this issue, there may be a followup Epic, or PRD.

summary: Remove appcelerator/titanium template
Dataset Clients should not be removed to avoid problems with deferred updates for inactive clients
description:
*What*
Make changes to the code so that inactive dataset clients will not be removed immediately from the db
*Why*
At the moment, when a dataset client is being inactive (no client has accessed it for a period time), the dataset client will be removed & the records of the dataset client will be checked and cleaned up. However, this has caused a few issues:
1. if there are some deferred sync requests, there is a chance the dataset client is being deleted completed by the time the sync request is being processed (Related to 
2. the delete dataset client operation is an expensive operation. If the inactive period is set too low, it could have an impact on the performance of the system.
3. If the dataset client back later on, the whole datasetclient & dataset client records have to be recreated again.
Based on those issues, it's better not to delete the dataset client when a dataset client become inactive.
*How*
* We will leave them in the database but will not sync them with the backend, until the next sync request is invoked for those dataset clients.
* we will also create a repeat job that will check the dataset clients periodically, and delete them based on a configuration that can be set by the developer.

summary: Write a guide for configuring Sync processor intervals based on available stats
description:
*What*
Write a guide for configuring Sync processor intervals based on available stats
*Why*
So developers can tweak it to best manage the expected load of their app.
*How*
How to best manage the load depends on the developer too. For example, should it:
* continue to respond to client calls as quick as possible (high processor interval)
* prioritise pending updates (low pending processor interval)
The effect of changing the processor interval for each processor (sync, pending, ack) should be tested and understood as part of writing this guide.
Probably involves running some tests (e.g. `ab` or `vegeta` to get feedback on the behaviour).
We should use the stats endpoint to get feedback (Although you may get a better visual feedback with grafana)
The sync architecture may help with understanding what the processors are and what they do

summary: add caching for dataset client records to improve performance of the syncRecords API
description:
h3. Why
While running the load tests against the `syncAll` endpoint that is calling both `sync` and `syncRecords` API, we see a big drop in terms of performance. From the metrics, we can see most of the time is spent on read the dataset client and its records. Given that this data is only changing when the sync loop runs, we can add caching to improve the performance.
h3. What
1. introduce a configuration option to enable/disable the cache.
2. When enabled, cache the results from `doReadDatasetClientWithRecords` using redis. Invalidate the cache everytime when `doUpdateDatasetClientWithRecords` is called. Read the results from cache if possible.
full_text:
add caching for dataset client records to improve performance of the syncRecords API

h3. Why
While running the load tests against the `syncAll` endpoint that is calling both `sync` and `syncRecords` API, we see a big drop in terms of performance. From the metrics, we can see most of the time is spent on read the dataset client and its records. Given that this data is only changing when the sync loop runs, we can add caching to improve the performance.
h3. What
1. introduce a configuration option to enable/disable the cache.
2. When enabled, cache the results from `doReadDatasetClientWithRecords` using redis. Invalidate the cache everytime when `doUpdateDatasetClientWithRecords` is called. Read the results from cache if possible.

summary: introduce backoff strategies for workers to reduce the resource usage of the sync server
description:
h3. Why
While doing the load testing, I noticed that if the worker interval is set to a relative low value, it will increase the load on the sync server, even when there is nothing to process in the queue.
Given that the app will do other things as well, the sync server should not consume that much resource when there is no jobs to run. We should slow down the worker interval when there is no jobs to process, and then set it to the normal rate once the jobs are created.
h3. What
we should introduce a backoff strategies for workers. This will kick in once there are no jobs to process. It will be reset once there are jobs created again.
Developers should be able to override the configuration for each worker.

summary: investigate if it's possible to run another app to process the data generated by the existing app
description:
h3. Why
This is a request from the customer (Simense). The idea is that the existing app will be responsible for accepting requests and put the data in the database. Another app will be created to process the data from the database as quickly as possible. 
There are a few benefits if we can support this:
1. another options to scale the sync server even further
2. allow developer to separate HTTP requests handling vs. sync processing. Changes to any one of them will not affect the other.
h3. What
Investigate if this is possible. Based on the current design, it should be. We need to:
* allow developers to override the mongodb url and redis url via env var
* in fh-mbaas-api, when those env vars exist, pass them to the `sync.connect` method
* in theory, that should be it. The sync server should then take the jobs from the same data base as the existing app and process them.
However, we do need to do some testing to confirm this, and see if there are anything else we didn't think of.

summary: Allow concurrent tasks to be taken from the queue by a single worker
description:
*What*
Allow concurrent tasks to be taken from the queue by a single worker
*Why*
To allow a developer to make better use of the CPU(s) in the event of slow asynchronous tasks.
For example, a dataset backend is quite slow (5 seconds per request), and there is only 1 cloud app running with no clustering or multiple pods.
This would mean there is at least 5 seconds between each item being taken off the queue and being processed. While an item is being processed, the CPU is relatively idle as it is waiting for the dataset backend to respond.
The single worker processes items on the queue synchronously.
Currently, the only way to have multiple items on the queue being processed at the same time is to scale up to multiple workers via cluster forking or by running multiple Pods. However, that would be inefficient in this example as the CPU is being underutilised.
It would be more efficient to process multiple items on the queue at the same time in that 1 worker as there is enough CPU cycles available to do that.
*Suggestions*
* add a worker concurrency flag, with a default value of 1
* add tests for changing the flag and verify it behaves as expected

summary: optimise sync mongodb data pruning
description:
h3. Why
The sync framework need to prune the following data it's creating:
* queue messages
* datasetClients and records data
At the moment, the approach to implement this is to have a function runs every x minutes and remove the data.
This does cause some problems:
* extra configurations that developers need to understand
* when there are multiple workers running, it's possible to cause race conditions
h3. What
To address these problems, we can:
* consider using mongodb TTL to remove old data. This is especially useful for queue messages
* try make sure only 1 worker will remove the dataset clients and it's records.

summary: Spike MCP authenticating via RHSSO using OSCP as Oauth Provider
description:
*Why*
We want a unified and standard way of doing authentication. RHSSO is the chosen product to integrate with.
We should also look to use a standard authentication and authorisation method. OSCP supports oauth2 and we want to investigate using OSCP as an oauth provider via RHSSO as we will need to heavily interact with the OSCP API from MCP.
*How*
Deploy an RHSSO in OSCP
Configure it to use OSCP as an oauth2 provider
Investigate if there is an RHSSO js client that we can use.
We should reach out to the RHSSO team for more information.
Prove some kind of interaction with OSCP (IE listing resources such as Services)
We may be able to achieve this without the actual MCP web client spike as it can be done as a standalone investigation.

summary: Spike creating mobile apiserver for serving mobile Objects in OpenShift.
description:
*What*
We want to represent mobile client applications in OSCP. 
*Why*
The MCP is focused around mobile applications and OSCP. In order to provide contextual information, we will need to represent the mobile app and potentially each type of mobile client (andriod, ios) in some kind of data structure so that we can provide a compelling UI.
*How*
While we could do this in a custom server side that is deployed with the MCP, every MCP is going to need to represent these objects. Kubernetes allows extending its API for exactly this kind of purpose. They have both a CustomResource definition and custom apiserver. 
*Goal*
Understand how to create a custom apiserver
Understand how to install the server and the permissions required.

summary: Investigate improper SplashScreenActivity FH initialization
description:
*Why?*
I found that in multiple templates (at least sync-android-app, pushstarter-android-app) there is improper initialization of FH SDK. 
_FH.init()_ is called when splash screen activity is displayed. When you have some other activity displayed and it goes to the background, Android can then kill the process. You can then return to the activity and in this case new app process is created, it jumps to the previously displayed activity and splash screen with initialization is skipped. This causes app to crash - see FH-3773 for more details.
*What to do?*
* investigate all Android native templates and check where it's happenning
* create tasks for fixing the problem

summary: Spike using the OpenShift web console extensions and pattern fly launcher for the MCP UI
description:
*What*
Explore what can be done with the OpenShift UI extensions. 
- Can we provide a full mobile set of views with navigation etc
- Can we customise the new app screen inside a namespace to have a (launch mobile control panel option)
Document how we would approach installing and developing this extension. 
Document Any limitations that we need to be aware of.
Document the perms required for adding this extension to an OSCP cluster
*Why*
MCP UI is going to be heavily integrated into OpenShift. It will rely largely on the OSCP API. Being able to launch the MCP UI as an extension which would provide the mobile centric view has several advantages:
- We would be in the same domain (so would have access to all tokens and cookies)
- It would avoid a double login
- The user would not need to install anything, they would simple launch the mobile view
How
Read through the docs outlined below and see can you get a sample customisation working and a sample launcher working. Reach out the OpenShift team for help if needed. 
Then build out more complex functionality (mock data is fine for now).
*Note* The full extent needs to be hashed out further.

* return all required configuration (binding credentials) data to allow:
** generation of the client SDK config
** services to mount the credentials and use them in their configuration
** generate a signover URL for administering the realm

summary: Dynamically mount the Keycloak binding secret into the Sync Service
description:
*What*
Dynamically mount the Keycloak binding secret into the Sync Service via a mobile-server api
*Why*
So Sync can read the secret/credentials and talk to keycloak to authenticate sync client users
*How*
* Add server-side logic to the API Server to read the secret for the service
* If the secret is a Keycloak secret update the Sync service deployment to mount that secret, thereby triggering a redeploy of Sync Service to pick up on the keycloak config.
** For the e2e, it is OK for the deployment change to redeploy automatically. But we may want to restrict this for production scenarios.

summary: Investigate not requiring cluster admin perms for server installation.
description:
*What*
Currently to install we need clusteradmin permissions to create cluster role binding and register the api server. These binding give us the permissions needed to delegate authentication to kubernetes and read specified certs etc. We want the MCP to be as easy to install as possible and so want to investigate ways of doing similar things without the need for the cluster perms.
*How*
Investigate how the Jenkins openshift plugin works (this doesn't require cluster admin perms to install) and see can we translate what it is doing into something that makes sense for us. 
We need to be able to protect our custom APIs and objects. The level of authorisation we need is likely just to check the requesting user has read perm on the current namespace for listing and reading and edit permission for changing creating etc.

summary: Research User Interaction Anomaly Detection Approaches for Mobile
description:
I think we should consider doing User Interaction Anomaly detection research. 
This would basically mean that we build up a record of user interactions in the app, so we can see their typical usage flows and build up a trust score. If we begin to see UI actions that are different from the users normal interactions (ie. lots of requests to sensitive areas or otherwise) then it will lower the trust score. If the trust score goes too low, we should block user actions/ask to re-authenticate.
It might be a good idea to research best approaches and discover if there are any existing libraries.

summary: Call to OpenShift on startup to get the server metadata
description:
*Why*
The mcp will use OpenShift as an oauth provider.
When the mcp is deployed on OpenShift, it would make for a poor installation/setup if the user had to manually configure the OpenShift URL.
The OpenShift Master host is exposed as an IP address via an env var (KUBERNETES_MASTER_HOST), but this IP address will not work when sending users to it for oauth authorization. The OpenShift public hostname must be used.
*How*
On mcp startup, make a call to the server metadata endpoint [1]. Based on the response:
* set the appropriate config for the server oauth client [2]
* build the config.js response for the /console/config.js endpoint [3]
The mcp startup should fail if:
* there is no response or an error/invalid response
* the scopes_supported, response_types_supported or grant_types_supported don't include the values used in mcp i.e.
** scopes - user:info user:check-access
** response_types - code token
** grant_types - authorization_code
[1] 
[2] 
[3]

summary: [Spike, clientsdk] Determine how to consume MCP KeyCloak configuration in a client SDK
description:
Services are enabled and configured and exposed via well known URLs and json config files. The build tools should check this config object and validate the current apis and implementation against it.
We have three coarse options : 
 * A build system plugin that downloads this file and sets up the client SDK at compile time
 * APIs in the SDK that downloads this file at runtime and sets up the app
 * An external tool that can make fill out a template like millicore does for 3.x
This spike will, among other things, determine which option we take.

summary: [Spike, clientsdk] Investigate Keycloak Login Screen Related Functionality Compatibility with a Custom Login Screen
description:
h6. What
The Keycloak login interface features a lot more functionality and features than a traditional login screen. For example:
# 2FA
# User Actions Post Auth
# Brute force detection and lockouts
# Audit of login events
# Social logins
# etc
In Keycloak default login screen on the server, a lot of features in Keycloak are bound to this login interface. If we use out our own login screen, we will break the relationship between the login screen and the keycloak backend features.
If we are going to create out own custom login screens, we should investigate if is possible during authentication if we can manually call endpoints on Keycloak to retrieve/report on the following so we can properly handle them in the mobile client login interface:
* *2FA*
* Has the user setup a 2FA token
* Is this credential type currently enabled
 * *User Actions Post Auth*
* Does the user need to update his profile after login?
* Does the user need to configure OTP after login?
* Does the user need to verify his email after login?
* Does the user need to update his password after login?
* *Brute force detection*
* Is brute force detection enabled in Keycloak for this client?
* What are the maximum amount of retries/intervals between retries etc ?
* Is there a temporary or permanent lockout in place?
* Does keycloak have an endpoint that we can report a lockout too?
* *Audit of Login Events*
* Does keycloak have an endpoint where we can submit login events to the server.
These are some quick examples, but there is likely many more..
h6. Why
If we move to use our own custom login screens instead on the mobile clients, it could break compatibility of a number of key features in Keycloak. This would essentially be re-writing the Keycloak auth features on the login screen in the different mobile platforms - Android, iOS, Cordova.

summary: Setup a 'Hybrid' MCP using UI extensions & server per namespace
description:
*What*
The 'hybrid' approach will leverage OpenShift UI extensions for the UI,
and the deployment of an mcp server per namespace.
The UI will need to talk to the mcp server in that namespace for working with 'Mobile Apps' and 'Mobile Enabled Services'.
*Why*
This approach is based on the first & second phases of the POC.
For the first phase
* the UI was 'in' OpenShift via a UI extension
* the server was a 'kubernetes api server'
* it stored 'mobileapp' resources in etcd
* the server was registered with the kubernetes API Aggregator to extend the kubernetes API
For the second phase
* the UI was completely standalone
* the UI used oauth to login to openshift to get a token 
* the server was deployed per namespace
* the server required a serviceaccount token
* mobile apps were represented as a 'configmap'
* services were represented as a 'secret'
The UI in OpenShift via UI extensions was chosen as the better UX as it made Mobile more discoverable i.e. a Mobile tab in the left nav.
The Server per namespace was chosen as it avoids unnecessary admin privileges required to install the server at the 'cluster level'.
*How*
Combine the UI approach from the first phase with the server approach from the second phase.

summary: spike secret creation for adding external services to an mcp instance
description:
*What*
A Mobile service can be provisioned in to any namespace. Something like keycloak could already exist outside of OSCP. These services are not forced to be in the same namespace as the mcp. However we will still want to provide integrations to these services and represent them in the mcp UI.
*How*
Mobile services are currently represented by the existence of a secret that has the name of the known mobile service in it. To represent an external service we will want to create a secret in the same namespace as the mcp that has the required details for targeting that external service from the mcp and mobile clients. This secret should have a label or annotation to flag it as external. 
A usecase we can work from is:
I do not want to provision a keycloak into every namespace, I want it to be shared across my mobile projects and consumed by several mobile clients.
It is worth noting that in a situation where sync is provisioned in the mcp namespace and keycloak in another we would need to create a public client and bearer only client to allow sync to be protected by the keycloak server
In a situation where sync is provisioned in a different namespace and keycloak in a different namespace and mcp in a third namespace, I don't think we can support protecting the sync server with keycloak. Perhaps adding docs to instruct a developer what they need to do in order to manually mount the config would be an option here.
Another usecase is :
I have a custom app with a rest api and I want to integrate it into my mobile client. In this case the mcp ui would allow them to create a custom service with a name and the location and credentials etc which would then be created as a secret in the namespace.

summary: Review binding policy for keycloak apb
description:
Currently we use a hard-coded secret name in the keycloak apb, to avoid using the openshift binding system - this is because the user might opt-out of creating the binding and then the service would be invisible to the MCP.
It would be preferable to use the built-in Openshift binding system rather than re-engineering all of this existing solution, it would also be preferable that the {{keycloak-apb}} only creates elements required for keycloak, rather than elements for "keycloak for mobile".
It might be possible to set some values in the {{apb.yml}} file, or elsewhere, that remove the option to opt-out of creating the binding and instead always generate it.

summary: Build Farm Installation via Ansible Service Broker
description:
*What*
Figure out how to install the build farm in the current namespace without needing user interaction during the installation
*Why*
So the build farm can be installed in a repeatable manner for 5.x users
*How*
* Install the Build Farm to an OpenShift cluster to better understand how it works
 
there is a digger art which will perform an android debug build.
* How much can be re-purposed as an Ansible Playbook Bundle for use in the Service Catalog via the Ansible Service Broker
* Identify any parts of the installation that require manual intervention, and ways to automate/workaround them for provisioning from the Service Catalog
** Acceptance of the Android SDK Licence
** Copying of a public key to Jenkins via the Jenkins UI
** Configuring the installer to use http to avoid SSL cert issues when talking to the Jenkins API (non-production/local use)
* Identify reasons for the installer to call the Jenkins API. (Can these be avoided by building all requirements into the base jenkins image, or configuring the image via env vars or startup arguments?) (add follow up tasks based on this)
** Document all calls to the Jenkins API
* Identify what Jenkins plugins the build farm uses
** Ensure the OpenShift auth plugin is enabled
** Document all plugins
* The MCP PoC will make the assumption that the Build Farm is in the current namespace. Other possible configurations can be explored after the PoC if required e.g. a completely external Buildfarm shared by many projects.
* The Build Farm shows up in the Service Catalog under the Mobile category.

summary: Add Build Farm integration to the MCP Server
description:
*What*
Expose endpoints from the MCP server to manage builds via the Build Farm
*Why*
So MCP users can use the Build Farm for building their Mobile Apps
*How*
What does OpenShift do when it creates/triggers a BuildConfig for a pipeline? Will this avoid the need for interacting with jenkins completely?
Based on this answer, the below may not all be needed
* Provisioning the build farm to the same namespace as the MCP server should auto-configure the MCP server to be aware of the Build Farm (or MCP should auto-discover the Build Farm) (via secrets)
* New endpoints will be needed for managing builds & build logs, build credentials, repo urls, repo credentials
* Generate a pub/priv key pair and tell the user to add the pub key to their repo (store them as secrets)
* The repo url should be associated with their app
* 'Build credentials' management (associated with an app) i.e. certificate & key for Android (store them as secrets)
* Creating the jenkins job for the app when a build is triggered (if not already done)
* Return a url for build info/logs possbily proxying through to the build farm for downloading the artifacts and logs
See the digger client usage code in millicore for an example of how some of this is done 
Possible to use/build upon or other existing clients?

summary: MCP UI Integration with the Build Farm
description:
*What*
Add a bulid farm integration to the MCP UI
*Why*
So MCP users can use the Build Farm for managing App builds
*How*
(Mockups/screens to follow from Brid, but shouldn't hold up implementation/wiring up)
* The Build Farm will show up as a Enabled in the MCP Overview screen. This type of service is different from fh-sync-server or keycloak in that it a Mobile App runtime service i.e. Mobile Apps will not depend on it at runtime. This is still a valid service to show in the MCP Overview screen though as it forms part of the overall Mobile solution. As the Build Farm is not a Mobile App runtime service, appropriate changes should be made to the sdk init endpoint in the MCP server to ensure Build Farm credentials are not sent to Mobile Apps on startup
* A new tab in the Mobile App screen
This will allow configuration of build credentials for the App in context e.g. App repo, Repo key, Certificate & Key for building, Provisioning Profile (if iOS)
* A new tab in the Mobile App screen
This will show a view, similar to the existing > view in Any sub-screens of the Pipelines view will actually follow through the > sub-screens already in OpenShift (for the POC at least), or to Jenkins e.g. for build logs
* A new tab in the Mobile Service screen for the Build Farm.
Similar to the Mobile App Build above, this will show a Pipelines view of all known Build Pipelines for apps in that the Build Farm knows about.
* Show Build Farm configuration on the existing Service > screen. This may not require any extra work other than ensuring a is created to store the Build Farm credentials & url.

summary: Add createbuild end-point to mcp-api
full_text:
Add createbuild end-point to mcp-api

*What*
Create a new end-point in the mcp-api server which will create a new buildconfig in the namespace that the mcp-api server is running against. If the repo is private then we will create a keypair and return the public key as part of this end-points response.
Make a secret for the build-config which will store the public/private keypair and the app-id this is a buildconfig for and the buildconfig-id.
*How*
This end-point should be a {{POST}} to {{/build}}, with the following JSON body:
{code}
{
 "app_id": "<id of app this build is for",
 "jenkins_file": "<path-to-jenkins-file>",
 "repo_is_private": <boolean>,
 "git": {
 "repo": "<git-repo>",
 "branch": "<git-branch-name>",
 "auth": "<git-auth-key>",
 },
 "build_credentials_secret_name": "<build_credentials_secret>",
 "extra_params": {
 "<user_defined_param>": "<custom_value>",
 "<user_defined_param>": "<custom_value>"
 }
}
{code}
This will create a new buildconfig with the specified values.
*Note* we will also need to map the params set by the current millicore implementation to be env vars in the jenkinsfile

The archiving of build artefacts is controlled by the Jenkinsfile. This means we need to discover the artefact url.

The build object created from the build config, has a status field that has the jekins url we need to call in it:
By watching the build object we will be able to retrieve the url to get the build artefacts. The response from this Jenkins API is :
{code}
[{"id":"n1","name":"android-debug.apk","path":"platforms/android/build/outputs/apk/android-debug.apk","url":"/job/localmcp-androidapp1/1/artifact/platforms/android/build/outputs/apk/android-debug.apk","size":4360173}]
{code}

summary: Look at extending the Jenkins sync plugin to sync secrets
description:
*What*
We need to be able to specify secrets that contain build credentials as part of a build config and have them synced to Jenkins as credentials.
Credentials for doing App Builds (e.g. developer certificates, keys, profiles) can be added to Jenkins as Credentials (similar to done for the 4.x build farm by millicore ). However, with the 5.x build farm integration looking to leverage the OpenShift Jenkins integration (the OpenShift Sync plugin) as much as possible. be adding/updating OpenShift resources and let the OpenShift Sync plugin take care of creating/updating things in Jenkins. summary: [UI] Android Release Build
description:
*What*
Build on the work in FH-4154 (and optionally FH-4190 for a private repo) to allow doing a release build with Cert/Key credentials.
*Why*
So a user can get an Android Release build (APK) through the MCP & Build Farm integration.
*How*
Change the Edit screen to allow:
* Setting the Certificate & Key Secrets to use for the Build (via a Dropdown)
* The Dropdown can show all available mcp-build secrets, and an 'Upload' Option
* Uploading a Certificate or Key (to the MCP) which get saved as Secrets, and linked to the BuildConfig
* The linking of the Secret & BuildConfig will be done by labeling e.g.
** type=mcp-build (For Build Credentials like Keys & Certs)
** mcp-build-id=<build_config_id>
** type=mcp-src (For Repo Key
** mcp-src-id=<build_config_id>
Change the View screen to show:
* the Certificates and Keys linked to the Build
* the secret name/id is sufficient, which should come back in the BuildConfig data
* the Cert/Key secret name can be a link to the actual Secret (i.e. the Secret screen in OpenShift)
See example branch of the sync/keycloak demo cordova app for a repo that has a simple Jenkinsfile for an Android Debug Build 
This Jenkinsfile will need to be modified to use Jenkins Credentials (as created by the OpenShift Sync plugin in FH-4153 based on the Certificate & Key Secrets)

summary: Allow temporary download url to be generated
description:
*What*
To allow someone to send a link to allow build to be downloaded, we want to create a temporary token that will be used as part of an mcp url to allow downloading the binary.
*How*
Add an endpoint to the server for creating build download url. This endpoint will generate a token and attach it as a annotation to to the specified app build. It will also create a timestamp on the build for when the token will become invalid. 
Then it will return an MCP url for downloading the binary with the token appended as a query param.
In a second endpoint, we will check the token and the timestamp on the build. If valid we will use our service account token to proxy through to Jenkins and retrieve the artefact.

summary: [UI] Allow Users to generate & show a build artifact download URL in the UI
description:
*What*
Using the server logic in FH-4215, allow the user to generate an artifact download url & present it in the UI.
*Why*
So users can download a build artifact to their device without requiring additional auth steps.
This will facilitate easy install of binaries, and speed up the Users development flow.
*How*
* On the 'Mobile App' > 'Build History' tab, show a button beside each build to 'Generate a Unique Download URL'.
* Include info on what this will do, and how long the URL will be valid for (see FH-4215 for details).
* This button will call to the MCP server to generate a download URL.
* The download URL will then be shown instead of the 'Generate' button.
* There will only be 2 states for this
** Either the 'Generate' button is shown as there is no download URL (or the download URL has expired). 
** Or the Download URL will be shown
* An option to show a QR code version of the Download URL can be shown. This could be a button beside the download URL link e.g. 'Show QR Code'

h6. What
We should implement Certificate pinning in a similar way to how it was done in the android template - we could consider using trustkit for this too - 
- This should also involve a preflight check to the auth server so that pinning can occur before the redirect to the system browser as a safeguard. An appropriate error message should be shown to warn the user that their connection is not secure. The auth button should also be disable or hidden.
TrustKit config to place in the info.plist top level, or use the AppDelegate.swift to define it manually.
{code:java}
	<key>TSKConfiguration</key>
	<dict>
		<key>TSKPinnedDomains</key>
		<dict>
  <key>osm1.skunkhenry.com</key>
  <dict>
  <key>TSKEnforcePinning</key>
  <true/>
  <key>TSKIncludeSubdomains</key>
  <true/>
  <key>TSKPublicKeyAlgorithms</key>
  <array>
  <string>TSKAlgorithmRsa2048</string>
  </array>
  <key>TSKPublicKeyHashes</key>
  <array>
  <string>jAoDAV3WG9IKcu0YJ1ZVTuEVqdcglfiQRqmfy3+ieoc=</string>
  <string>XAoDAV3WG9IKcu0YJ1ZVTuEVqdcglfiQRqmfy3+ieoc=</string>
  </array>
  </dict>
		</dict>
	</dict>
{code}

description:
This epic serves as a catch-all place for prototyping the testing infrastructure we need to have for successful development of our new mobile platform.
These are the assumptions that will guide the POCs:
* the primary delivery process for our services will be [ansible playbook bundles| deployed on openshift through [ansible service broker| which means that PR-testing of apb updates has high priority
* we expect the services to be capable of working stand-alone, which means that bulk of functional integration testing can happen outside of openshift
* we expect the mobile client libraries to be usable outside of the on-device mobile-runtime
* for any service(s)/openshift/mobile-clien(s) integration, there should be an end-to-end setup path, involving just cli/api use, not involving UI
* any js-based UI should have underlying api-library testable outside of browser
* all code should unit tests run on PRs, code-coverage metrics and only rising trend of code covered with PR's
End goal of this epic is to challenge, or validate these assumptions with POC tasks and prepare the tooling, infrastructure and environment for application of the valid assumptions.

summary: SPIKE running apb test for PR's with a Jenkins file on our jenkins-wendy CI cluster
description:
After figuring out the simple test in the previous spike, we should be able to create a PR check for apb repositories.
This means
* building the apb image (probably without apb tool)
* optionally uploading the built image to docker-registry
* running the image's test command (probably without apb tool)
* clean-up the test-project/artefacts after successful run
We shouldn't need to spawn new openshift to do this.
These sort of tests should take <10 minutes.
We should check if there wouldn't be too much load resulting from this on our CI jenkins.
Based on the results, we could try to spawn additional infrastructure, have this sort of basic deployment test behind comment/tag trigger, or rethink the testing strategy altogether.
The preferable thing would still be, to be able to run these sorts of tests on every PR to *-apb repos.

summary: Package the basic Jenkins jobs so they can be automatically created
description:
*What*
Create Jenkins Job Builder yaml files for all the pre-existing Jenkins jobs.
*Why*
The final system will need to be packaged in some way so that new users can quickly start using it with needing to configure it. The system will require some Jenkins jobs to exist before the user starts using it. e.g.
* a job to decrypt backup files
* a job to deploy a server with the relevant DBMS
* a job to import backups into the DBMS on the server
* a pipeline that performs a full single backup restoration
These jobs should not be configured by the user, they are the building blocks that enable a user to run restorations. Therefore there needs to be some automated method of creating and configuring these jobs when the user initially install/deploys the system.
*How*
[Jenkins Job Builder| can be used to define jobs as _yaml_ or _json_ files which can be used to create jobs on a Jenkins server.
